subject: mathematics
question_text: If A, B, C are angles of a triangle, then prove that cos2A + cos2B + cos2C = −1 − 4 cosA cosB cosC.

mark_split.label: Pair two terms with a sum-to-product formula
Apply the product formula and conclude

verification.note: Source: Baby Bullet-Q, Junior Inter Maths-1A (Sri Publishers, Machilipatnam), book p.39 — LAQ chapter 5 T-Ratios upto Transformations, answer 26.2. Printed appearances: AP 17 · TS 16. The twin of 26.1 on the same page. The −1 on the right comes from the double-angle form cos 2C = 2cos²C − 1, and it is the one thing that makes this proof differ from its partner. ⚠ THE MARK SPLIT IS OURS, NOT THE BOOK'S — no [N Marks] tags are printed anywhere in this chapter (its pages are set two questions to a page in two columns, which takes the margin those tags would occupy). The 1+2+2+1+1 above follows the shape of the split the same book DOES print for LAQ answer 23 on book p.37, weighting the two substantial transformations against the set-up and the finish. The SAME split and the SAME step ids are used on all eight answers in this chapter, deliberately: they are ONE method over different identities — pair two terms, use the angle condition, factor, finish with a product formula. A student who learns that arc once can attempt any of them. The book's chapter header carries ★★ and reads '7 Marks'; that star is the CHAPTER's rank, not this question's. This is a coaching publication, not a TSBIE document, so the split stays unverified until a Telangana IPE teacher confirms it. Paper position: Maths-1A Section C runs Q18-Q24 at 7 marks each, answer any 5 of 7; Q23 is the Transformations slot and is ALWAYS a question of this kind. Re-cut to the 8-mark Section-C form of the 2026-27 pattern (TGBIE model paper w.e.f. 2026-27): the extra mark goes to Pair two terms with a sum-to-product formula.

recall_prompt: Say how you would prove this identity — say the four moves in order, and where the angle condition gets used.

steps.label: State the angle condition
steps.margin_note: First mark. Same condition as the twin question. Write it first — both uses of it below depend on it.
steps.memory_tip: A + B = 180° − C. Write it first — both uses below depend on it.

recall.must_convey: That the angle condition is written down first, in the form the proof will actually use.
accept: write the angle condition first in the form the proof needs
state the given condition and rearrange it
note the angle sum before starting the transformation
modata angle condition rasi, kavalsina form lo pettali
write down the condition on the angles

steps.why: Without the condition the statement is simply false, so it is not preamble — it is the hypothesis the whole proof leans on, and it is used at least twice below.
common_mistakes: Starting the transformation before writing the condition.
Writing the condition but never rearranging it into a usable form.

steps.label: Pair two terms
steps.margin_note: Three of the eight marks. Three terms will not factorise as they stand, so two of them are combined into a product first. Quote the formula in brackets — the formulas are what the examiner marks.
steps.memory_tip: Pair cos2A with cos2B, and expand cos2C as 2cos²C − 1 so the −1 appears cleanly.

recall.must_convey: That the first two terms are paired with the cos C + cos D formula and the third expanded as 2cos²C − 1.
accept: pair the first two with cos C plus cos D and write cos two C as two cos squared C minus one
apply sum to product on the first pair and the double angle form on the third
use the cosine sum formula on two of them
modati rendu ki cos C plus cos D formula, moodava term two cos square C minus one
combine two terms and expand the third
heard_as: two cos squared C minus one

steps.why: Choosing 2cos²C − 1 rather than 1 − 2sin²C is deliberate: it is the form that produces the −1 the right-hand side needs.
common_mistakes: Using cos 2C = 1 − 2sin²C, which cannot produce the −1 cleanly.

steps.label: Use the condition
steps.margin_note: Two more marks. This is where the angle condition earns its place: it converts an expression in A and B into one in C, so that every term shares a factor.
steps.memory_tip: cos(180° − C) = −cos C, with the MINUS. That sign is the whole difference here.

recall.must_convey: That A + B becomes 180° − C, and that cos(180° − C) = −cos C, introducing the minus sign.
accept: replace A plus B by one eighty minus C and the cosine picks up a minus sign
cos of one eighty minus C is minus cos C
use the angle condition, the cosine becomes negative
cos one eighty minus C ante minus cos C
substitute and the sign flips

steps.why: Cosine changes sign across 180° where sine does not. That single difference is why this proof and its twin diverge here.

steps.label: Take the common factor out
steps.margin_note: Seventh mark. The common factor comes out, and the condition is used a SECOND time inside the bracket so that both bracket terms are the same kind of function.
steps.memory_tip: Take the common factor out and leave the −1 outside; a sign slip turns the bracket into a difference.

recall.must_convey: That −1 is separated out and −2cos C taken as the common factor, with cos C rewritten as −cos(A+B) so the bracket becomes a sum.
accept: pull the minus one out and take minus two cos C common, then cos C becomes minus cos A plus B so the bracket is a sum
separate the minus one and factor out two cos C
the bracket turns into cos A minus B plus cos A plus B
minus one veru chesi, minus two cos C common teeyyali
rewrite the cosine so the bracket adds instead of subtracting

steps.why: The −1 plays no further part, so setting it aside early keeps the rest of the line short and the factorisation visible.
common_mistakes: Trying to factor the −1 into the bracket.
Getting the sign wrong so the bracket becomes a difference.

steps.label: Apply the product formula
steps.margin_note: Last mark. One more sum-or-difference formula turns the bracket into a product, and the identity closes. Write "= R.H.S" so the examiner can see it landed.
steps.memory_tip: Use the SUM formula to get cosines. Losing the −1 at the last line is the usual slip.

recall.must_convey: That cos(A+B) + cos(A−B) = 2 cosA cosB is applied, giving −1 − 4 cosA cosB cosC.
accept: cos A plus B plus cos A minus B is two cos A cos B so the answer is minus one minus four cos A cos B cos C
the bracket becomes two cos A cos B giving minus one minus four cos A cos B cos C
apply the product formula and finish
two cos A cos B vasthundi, minus one minus four cos A cos B cos C
the final answer is minus one minus four cos A cos B cos C
heard_as: four cos A cos B cos C

steps.why: A SUM of two cosines is a product of two cosines, where a DIFFERENCE would give sines. Picking the right one of the pair is what this last line tests.
common_mistakes: Using the difference formula and getting sines.
Losing the −1 at the very end.

insider_note: Pair the first two, then use cos2C = 2cos²C − 1, which is where the −1 comes from. cos(180° − θ) = −cosθ is needed twice, and both minus signs matter.
